column3: At the end of a request's turn (save()) the proving thread's stream waits for every entered side stream before the request's state and failure words are taken. Each sub-proof joins its own side streams; this wait holds where one does not. Without both, a failure flag that a kernel raises late on a side stream counts for no request, which costs the whole batch its files, or for the request that has the next turn; and a late write lands in memory that the next request works in.

The same wait at a request's end (end()). Without it, and without the sub-proof's own join, a flag that is raised late is not in the word by which the request is judged: it counts for no request, and the whole batch loses its files.

column3: live_flags() waits for the whole GPU before it reads the failure words. Whoever reads them through it leans on this wait and joins no side stream first: cp_commit, the weight table's keeper, and cp_prove where it takes the flags that are no request's at a batch's end. cp_commit holds the key under which it draws the key file's coins to the key that a second, separately written text of the key schedule derives from the seed. The test around this call derives the key twice through one wrapper (derive_key_files()), so without the call a fault in that wrapper, such as a call of the wrong routine of the schedule, passes; and no verifier sees whether a coin is what the rule gives. (A fault inside the schedule's own routines is met at the start: the row on keys_own_test() below.)
The same for the key of each entry's making, before a coin is drawn under it. No other line of that routine derives the key a second time.

Before a byte of the key file leaves the process cp_commit asks whether any salt of the first table was handed to the comparison with the second writing. Nothing asks later whether this question was put. Without it a hand-over of salts that is lost goes unseen, and the salts are no longer held to the second writing.
The question of the row above, inside the routine that is called there.
The same question before a byte of an entry leaves the process, of the first table's salts and of the copy's.
The question of the row above, inside the routine that is called there.

Where cp_commit derives a stored table's key from the seed, the copy of the seed and the key that stand on the stack are erased as soon as the key's bytes are handed out. Without the line both stay in memory that the program uses again; every file comes out the same, and no run shows it.

Before cp_commit draws or reads a seed it runs the generator of the tables' masks and salts on known answers, on the host and in a kernel, and ends if one differs. An earlier line runs the host's half by itself. Without this line the kernel's half is not run: a generator that is wrong in a kernel on this machine is first met under the real seed, by the comparisons with the second texts, which hold every mask once and only a sample of the salts.

Two words of the block that RFC 8439 prints (section 2.3.2), to which both halves of that test hold the masks' block function. With the vector and its comparison gone, a block function that is not ChaCha20's, and agrees with the test's other known answers, passes at every start.

Two words of one of the six blocks that RFC 8439 prints (appendix A.1, test vector 3), to which the own test of the sub-proofs' coin routines holds their block function at a start, on the host and in a kernel. The six blocks are that test's only answers that come from neither of this tree's two writings of the rule. (The CPU test coins_rfc8439_test.cpp holds the host's text to the same vectors, and no kernel.)

Before cp_commit draws or reads a seed it runs, on known answers, the routines that lead from a seed to a key, and the sub-proofs' coin routines. A wrong key or coin verifies as a right one does and may hide nothing. (By the comment above the line cp_commit draws nothing from these routines: the keys' half is the one that counts here.)

column3: cp_prove's set-up calls the routine of the row above, heeds its answer, and does so directly before its front closes and it reads the seed. Without the first line cp_prove reads its seed and serves without these tests.

The two counting words on the GPU (slot pads that agree with the key's coins; filler cells that are zero) start at a value that differs from request to request, and the host subtracts it at the end. Requests of one shape have the same sums. With one start for all, a word that was not laid anew and on which nothing was counted holds just what the host expects, and both counts pass without having been made.

A request gets no proof unless as many filler cells were found to be zero as the plan has. The forward pass does not write these cells and the verifier does not pin them. Without the line a request in whose filler cells an earlier sub-proof's bytes have stayed gets its proof, with these bytes committed to.

A layer sub-proof lays a second time, by the runtime's own fills and copies, what set-up wrote into the layer sub-proofs' shared buffers. The first writing is one launch, and a launch that the GPU accepts and never runs leaves no error. Without the second writing old bytes then stay in the filler cells, where the count of the row above is all that stands against them, and wherever else the run reads what set-up laid.

Behind an attention sub-proof's forward pass cp_prove compares its cells of q, k, v and o with those that the layer sub-proof committed to. The sub-proof's messages are made from its own cells, so a stray write there gives a proof that the verifier refuses: without the look that proof reaches the client; with it the request fails and gets no proof.

column3: An attention sub-proof zeroes its five cell matrices a second time at its start, for the same case: the calling program's zeroing before each run is one launch too. Without it, and with that launch lost, only the count of zero filler cells (prover/request.cuh, finish_request()) stands against old bytes in the filler cells.

The head's sub-proof zeroes its three cell matrices: the first of two times. With one of the two gone, a single fill that the GPU accepts and never carries out leaves old bytes in the filler cells, where only the count of zero filler cells (prover/request.cuh, finish_request()) stands against them.
The second of the two times. (The pin ends in the first words of the comment behind the fills, which tell the two places apart.)

cp_commit fills the buffer for a norm's multipliers with NaNs before the launch that makes them from a model's files. If the GPU accepts that launch and never runs it, the range test behind it refuses the NaNs. Without the fill, what lay in that memory before may pass the range test and be taken for multipliers; then only the comparison of the integers' SHA-256 with wsums.txt (hf_commit.cu, check_the_weights()) stands between them and the commitment.
The same for synthetic weights, which tests and the examples use: there the conversion to integers raises its fault word at a NaN, and no list of sums stands behind it.

cp_prove does the same where it reads a norm from a model's files, and set-up's range test refuses the NaNs. Without the fill what lay in the buffer may pass that test (zeros do), and the service starts on other weights than the committed ones.
The same in cp_prove for synthetic weights.

CardTree::begin() zeroes the array of a GPU Merkle tree's digests when it allocates it: every vertex of a tree that keeps all vertices, the upper levels of a lean tree. Memory from the pool still contains what its last user wrote, which may be hidden values or masks. Without the line, a digest that a faulty GPU failed to write (one store, or the whole thread block that computes the top of a lean tree's subtree) keeps those 32 bytes, is hashed into the root, and can be sent as a sibling in a proof that the verifier accepts. A run without a fault gives the same files with and without the line.

It cannot suppress a store into a lean tree's upper levels.

column3: cp_commit zeroes the GPU memory in which it builds the Merkle tree of a stored table. PartMaker::parts() builds a part's levels at two places in the buffer V, which take turns, and zeroes both before the part's leaves are made. In the first part of a call the places still contain symbols of the encoded, masked table, which are hidden. Without the line, a digest of the leaves' level or of the level above it that a faulty GPU failed to write keeps 32 bytes of those symbols and is hashed into the root. Where that level is kept (-keep 0 for the leaves, 0 or 1 for the level above) the bytes go to the kept nodes and can be sent as a sibling in an opening that the verifier accepts. From -keep 2 on, which includes the default at the full size, neither level is kept, and only hashes over those bytes are. A run without a fault gives the same files with and without the line.

The scratch memory into which a unit of weights is decoded for the opening is zeroed first. With -overlap it holds what a request of a later batch left there. Without the zeroing, and with a decoding that the GPU never ran, these values are folded as weights into the opening of another batch. (A play saw that batch get no proof with and without the zeroing: no file showed what the line changes.)

At the end of every pass cp_prove zeroes the GPU memory in its record or gives it back what it held at set-up's end; the weights and what is declared as laid once are left alone. Without the line what the requests of a pass left lies there until the next request starts, so also while the batch's opening works and while the service waits; and the restoring at a request's start spares the other requests' state buffers, memory labelled as one request's own, and the scratch memory above the mark to which it reaches.
The answer of the look at an attention sub-proof's cells (prover/layer_prove.cuh, above) is heeded: the request gets "failed" under the own tests' bit.

column3: Before a byte of the key file leaves the process cp_commit asks that the coins which it has handed to the proof library are the program's own generator, which numbers its draws and works a draw out a second time by a separately written text. The library's looks at its random values (../blocks/iop/send.h, not_as_drawn(); send_prove()'s read-back; iop/base_case.h; iop/lin.h) ask nothing of a draw without a number: with another generator handed in, the looks at mask tables, random tails and masking words would compare nothing and say nothing, and the pads' look would compare with its own copy alone; every file would be the same and every verifier would say yes.

Before bytes of a batch's proofs leave the process cp_prove asks that the batch's coins are the program's own generator, which numbers its draws and works a draw out a second time by a separately written text, and holds a sample of what it has laid (prover/chain_coins.cuh, coins_hold()). The proof library's looks at its random values (../blocks/iop/send.h, not_as_drawn(); iop/base_case.h; iop/lin.h) ask nothing of a draw without a number: with another generator in the batch's place the looks at the shared chain's mask tables, random tails and masking words would compare nothing and say nothing, every proof would be the same and every verifier would say yes.

name_them() puts a batch's ids on the syncing thread's list only behind the end of the loop that names the batch's responses, so that a request that has left work/ has its whole batch in out/. With the ids on the list any sooner, the syncing thread can take a request out of work/ while a response of its batch is not yet named, and a front end that checks a batch as it lies in out/ would then check a part of it. If the naming breaks off, no id is queued.
